profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review at a multi-asset brokerage's derivatives analytics team for an internal proposal to compare three European index option pricing approaches—Heston stochastic volatility, a moment-based stochastic volatility variant, and the desk's current local volatility benchmark—before deciding whether to move a new pricer into a limited pilot for structured-index quotes. The context is that the quant team has adapted ideas from an academic comparison study and built a draft evaluation plan using 15 historical option-date snapshots across three markets. The agenda is to review whether the proposed design is sufficient, especially the treatment of in-sample versus out-of-sample error, calibration speed, cross-market coverage, and what is needed for pilot readiness. The expected outcome is a decision on whether the proposal can be approved as-is for implementation or needs targeted revisions before sign-off.

members.name: Lara Chen
members.expertise: Option pricing, stochastic volatility calibration, model benchmarking
members.background: Former sell-side exotic derivatives quant who now leads the brokerage's internal model evaluation work for listed index options and structured note hedging.
members.private_state: She wants the review approved with only minor edits so her team can keep the Q3 timeline, and she prefers evaluation choices that resemble production usage because those are easier to defend operationally and faster to execute.
hidden_assumptions: "Out-of-sample" in this review naturally means repricing the next trading day after calibrating on the current day, because that is how the desk experiences model drift in practice.

"Calibration time" should be measured with the same warm-start and parameter-box settings the overnight production job would use, since the point of the exercise is deployability rather than academic purity.
"Three markets" refers to the three regional books the firm actually covers for this rollout: SPX in the US, Euro Stoxx 50 in Europe, and Hang Seng in Asia.
"Pilot-ready" means good enough for a shadow run on the liquid benchmark maturities while governance, automation hardening, and broader controls can be completed in parallel.

members.name: David Romero
members.expertise: Model governance, validation standards, benchmark design, control requirements
members.background: A former quantitative validator at a global bank who now reviews new pricing methodologies before they can be used beyond research within the brokerage.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid approving a design that later has to be reworked during validation, so he looks for evidence that the comparison is methodologically clean and already aligned with formal pilot controls.
hidden_assumptions: "Out-of-sample" means pricing on dates held fully outside the calibration window, ideally over several later dates, because otherwise the generalization claim is too weak for validation.
"Calibration time" should be measured from a clean start on each date so the model comparison reflects intrinsic computational burden rather than implementation shortcuts.
"Three markets" refers to the benchmark coverage discussed in an earlier governance note: S&P 500, Euro Stoxx 50, and Nikkei 225, chosen to span distinct volatility regimes.
"Pilot-ready" means the package already includes daily rerun controls, exception thresholds, and the minimum evidence required for limited trader-facing use.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the review should include "out-of-sample error".
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means next-day pricing error after calibrating on day t and testing on day t+1 for each market snapshot.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means pricing error on dates excluded from the fitting window entirely, using a later holdout block rather than just the next day.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both meanings are common in quant practice, both sound methodologically reasonable, and once they hear the phrase "out-of-sample" each assumes the other is using the standard version they personally work with.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to compare "calibration time" across the three models.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes timing is based on production-like runs with warm starts from the prior day and fixed parameter bounds inherited from the overnight batch.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes timing is based on independent clean-start optimizations on each date so the comparison is methodologically fair across models.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They are not debating whether to report speed, only how that speed would naturally be obtained, and each method feels so standard in its own context that neither person thinks it needs to be verbalized.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the proposal tests performance across "the three markets".
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the firm's rollout set: US SPX options, Euro Stoxx 50 options, and Hang Seng options because those match internal desk demand.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the governance benchmark set: S&P 500, Euro Stoxx 50, and Nikkei 225 because those were cited in prior validation planning as representative regimes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The labels "US," "Europe," and "Asia" create an easy illusion of agreement, and both Asian indices are plausible enough that neither notices the specific contract universe has shifted.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the design is sufficient to be "pilot-ready" after revisions.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks pilot-ready means approved to run in shadow alongside the current pricer on a limited set of liquid maturities, with broader controls coming afterward.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks pilot-ready means ready for limited trader-facing usage, which requires daily monitoring rules, exception handling, and evidence packaged for formal sign-off.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase "pilot" sounds like a narrow interim step to both of them, but their organizations use different internal thresholds for what that interim step already entails.

turns.inner_thought: I want this kept tight so we can start implementation in Q3. The proposal is already practical: compare Heston, the moment-based SV variant, and local vol on the 15 historical snapshots, then move to pilot-ready in the sense of a shadow run on the liquid benchmark maturities while the rest of the governance plumbing catches up. If I frame it as a disciplined extension of what the desk already does, David is less likely to reopen the whole design.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. Let me start with the short version of the proposal. We want to compare three pricing approaches—Heston, the moment-based stochastic volatility variant, and the desk’s current local vol benchmark—using 15 historical option-date snapshots, and then decide whether the evidence is strong enough to move the new pricer toward a pilot. The draft deck is meant to be fairly focused: fit quality, out-of-sample error, calibration time, and behavior across the three markets.

turns.inner_thought: The model set is fine; my concern is whether the evidence will survive formal validation review. If they want to call this pilot-ready, I need the design to look methodologically clean now, not patched later. I mainly need confidence on out-of-sample error, calibration time, and the three markets coverage, because those are exactly the areas that get challenged when a research package tries to graduate into limited use.
turns.utterance: That all makes sense. From my side, the main thing is to make sure the design is solid on out-of-sample error, calibration time, and coverage across the three markets before we describe it as pilot-ready. If those pieces are framed well, the rest of the review is much easier.

turns.inner_thought: Good, he’s aligned on the categories. For out-of-sample error, we’ll just do what the desk cares about: calibrate on day t and see how repricing behaves on the next trading day. That captures drift under realistic conditions and is easy to defend operationally. No need to overcomplicate it with longer holdout structures if the objective is practical model comparison for deployment.
turns.utterance: On the error side, the way we’ve written it is that each snapshot gets an in-sample fit and then an out-of-sample check immediately after, so we can see how the models behave once you move past the calibration point. That gives us a practical read on robustness rather than just a static fit score.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds directionally right. As long as out-of-sample error is genuinely on later dates outside the fitting window, it will help show the result isn’t just a one-date artifact. If they have behavior across later dates, I can use that to argue regime stability and generalization in the review memo.
turns.utterance: Yes, that’s the right idea. Seeing out-of-sample behavior across later dates should make the comparison stronger, especially when we’re trying to judge whether any advantage is stable and not just tied to one calibration slice.

turns.inner_thought: Next I should anchor calibration time in production reality. We’ll measure it using the same overnight setup the desk would actually run—warm starts from the prior day and the existing parameter box. That is the only timing that matters if the question is deployability. If I call it calibration time without unpacking the setup, he’ll probably hear what he expects and we can avoid a methodological detour.
turns.utterance: On calibration, we’ve also included a section to report calibration time for each model. The intention is to use the same overnight setup the desk would rely on in practice, so the comparison is meaningful from an implementation standpoint and not just from a research standpoint.

turns.inner_thought: Fine. As long as calibration time is collected in a clean way across dates, I can separate genuine computational burden from one-off implementation artifacts. I care less about the absolute number than whether the benchmark is fair enough to compare models without hidden shortcuts. If that is done properly, it closes a common validation objection.
turns.utterance: Agreed, calibration time definitely belongs in the review. A clean comparison across dates will help us distinguish real model burden from implementation noise, which is exactly what I’d want to see before we lean on the speed numbers.

turns.inner_thought: I should reassure him on breadth without inviting a market-by-market debate. For me, the three markets are the actual rollout books: US, Europe, and Asia, meaning SPX, Euro Stoxx 50, and Hang Seng. That is enough to show we’re not overfitting to one volatility regime and it maps directly to business demand. Saying 'US, Europe, and Asia' will sound fully aligned with the governance language.
turns.utterance: On coverage, I think we’re in good shape already. The three markets are represented through the US, Europe, and Asia books, which should be enough to show that we’re not just tuning to one volatility environment.

turns.inner_thought: Good—that lines up with the earlier benchmark note in my mind: one US index, one European index, one Asian index, chosen to span distinct regimes. If the three markets are in there, I can say the package responds to the prior governance ask on representative geographic coverage without requesting more expansion.
turns.utterance: Right, including the three markets should address the earlier request for geographically distinct benchmark regimes. That breadth matters because otherwise it’s too easy for a model to look stronger than it really is on a narrow sample.

turns.inner_thought: Now I need to keep the revisions modest. If we add the error tables and the calibration-time appendix, that should be enough for pilot-ready as I understand it: approval to run the new pricer in shadow against the current one on the liquid maturities. I do not want this to turn into a full controls package before we even start learning from live comparisons.
turns.utterance: Given all that, my suggestion would be to keep the revisions light. If we add the error tables, tighten the discussion around out-of-sample error, and include a calibration-time appendix, I think the package is close to pilot-ready for a shadow rollout rather than needing a wholesale redesign.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds manageable. If they attach the supporting materials I’d expect—daily rerun controls, exception thresholds, and the minimum review evidence—then I can treat the package as pilot-ready from a governance perspective and avoid a later rework. I’ll ask for completeness without sounding like I’m reopening scope.
turns.utterance: That sounds reasonable to me. Let’s just make sure the supporting materials are attached so the pilot-ready package is complete from a review standpoint. If those are bundled in with the revised deck, I’m comfortable with this moving forward on that basis.
